A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Darwin Gödel Machine study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite reformatting and appendix reordering.

before.justification: v1 reports original SWE-bench and Polyglot experiments, component ablations, model and language transfer evaluations, and a tool-hallucination case study.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds cross-benchmark transfer, a greedy-selection ablation, generated-agent functionality statistics, and a repeated-run Polyglot summary.

M1.justification: The DGM self-modification/evaluation loop, parent-selection rule, frozen models, tools, prompts, and generated-agent code are retained. Revised pseudocode clarifies the existing procedure. DGM Greedy is an additional comparison ablation, not a replacement for the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions cover SWE-bench Verified, multilingual Polyglot, Python-to-other-language transfer, and tool-use hallucination. The new cross-benchmark evaluations reuse these existing task populations with different search/evaluation assignments; they add no datasets, languages, or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds DGM Greedy, which always selects the best-performing parent, to comparisons on both benchmarks (Appendix A.3, Table 1). The existing two DGM ablations, OpenHands + CodeAct v2.1, and Aider remain. Newly supplied pseudocode for existing baselines does not add further comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces reciprocal held-out evaluation: search on one benchmark and evaluate the discovered agent on the other. It also reports the fraction of generated agents retaining code-editing functionality. Existing task lists, staged evaluation thresholds, pass@1 settings, model assignments, and main search budgets are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands validation with cross-benchmark generalization tests, a greedy-parent ablation testing whether branching beyond the best agent matters, and analysis of functional offspring production (Figure 4; Appendix A.3–A.4). Earlier model/language transfer, editor-implementation comparisons, and hallucination/objective-hacking analyses remain; the relocated Polyglot model-transfer plot is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: v1 discusses stochastic performance but provides no comparable across-run uncertainty summary. v2 newly reports three Polyglot DGM runs, with mean accuracy 40.7% and standard deviation 2.3 percentage points (Appendix A.4). This reporting remains limited to Polyglot, without corresponding baseline uncertainty or seed details.

E6.justification: Headline results remain unchanged. Added results include cross-benchmark transfer scores of 28.9% on Polyglot and 24.5% on SWE-bench, Greedy scores of 39.7% and 30.0%, functional-agent rates of 51.3% versus 32.5% for both original ablations, and the Polyglot run summary. Table 1 newly lists 14.0% for Polyglot without open-ended exploration, while retained Figure 2 shows a best score near 18%; this unexplained mismatch does not establish a same-setting performance decline.

T1.justification: The parent-selection definitions and equations (1)–(7) are unchanged between v1 Appendix A.2 and v2 Appendix C.2. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims of empirical self-improvement through archive-based exploration, superiority over the two original ablations, and the same headline benchmark improvements. The frozen-model scope remains explicit in the main text. Added validation supports these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and qualifications: cross-benchmark transfer is presented as evidence against benchmark-specific overfitting, and Appendix C.3 discusses private-test memorization risk and the separate diagnostic model. Appendices E.1 and I add baseline-cost tradeoffs, explain constraints on evolving the exploration process, and discuss alternative roles for human involvement.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses temperature 1.0, supplies pseudocode for both existing baselines, clarifies diagnostic-model responsibilities, and estimates approximately USD 10,000 per original baseline run versus the retained USD 22,000 DGM estimate. These are documentation additions, not established changes to the original settings. Task lists, code patches, and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against program synthesis, including neural/LLM-guided synthesis, and expands evolutionary-genetics, neural self-reference, and search-method connections. Appendix B distinguishes producing externally specified programs from modifying an agent's own implementation. Earlier cited work is retained, including material moved from the main open-endedness review.

P1.justification: The retained narrative receives abstract tightening, selected paragraph edits, and terminology changes such as 'initial agent' to 'base agent.' The main section sequence remains stable. Detailed related work and supplementary results are reorganized into earlier appendices, while most existing technical prose and code listings are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different document template and substantially reorganizes displays. Figure 4 gains a cross-benchmark panel and revised legends; its former Polyglot model-transfer panel becomes Figure 7. Tables 1–3 and two baseline algorithm displays are added, while existing supplementary plots move ahead of the algorithmic details.

improvement.justification: The cross-benchmark tests and greedy ablation strengthen v1's evidence for generalization and archive-based exploration. The run summary and implementation disclosures also improve transparency. These gains are bounded by limited uncertainty reporting and incomplete reconciliation of results: Table 1's 14.0% Polyglot baseline score is unexplained against Figure 2's approximately 18% best score. Overall, the additions provide a useful but limited quality improvement.
